speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy has made good progress toward our dual-mandate objectives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased from its highs without a significant increase in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s very good news.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But inflation is still too high, ongoing progress in bringing it down is not assured, and the path forward is uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I want to assure the American people that we’re fully committed to returning inflation to our 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Restoring price stability is essential to achieve a sustained period of strong labor market conditions that benefit all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today, the FOMC decided to leave our policy interest rate unchanged and to continue to reduce our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Over the past two years, we’ve significantly tightened the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our strong actions have moved our policy rate well into restrictive territory, and we’ve been seeing the effects on economic activity and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As labor market tightness has eased and progress on inflation has continued, the risks to achieving our employment and inflation goals are moving into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will have more to say about monetary policy—about monetary policy, after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indicators suggest that economic activity has been expanding at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: GDP growth in the fourth quarter of last year came in at 3.3 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For 2023 as a whole, GDP expanded at 3.1 percent, bolstered by strong consumer demand as well as improving supply conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Activity in the housing sector was subdued over the past year, largely reflecting high mortgage rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: High interest rates also appear to have been weighing on business fixed investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market remains tight, but supply and demand conditions continue to come into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Over the past three months, payroll job gains averaged 165,000 jobs per month, a pace that is well below that seen a year ago but still strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate remains low at 3.7 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Strong job creation has been accompanied by an increase in the supply of workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor force participation rate has moved up, on balance, over the past year, particularly for individuals aged 25 to 54 years, and immigration has returned to pre-pandemic levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nominal wage growth has been easing, and job vacancies have declined.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Although the jobs-to-workers gap has narrowed, labor demand still exceeds the supply of available workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased notably over the past year but remains above our longer-run goal of 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Total PCE prices rose 2.6 percent over the 12 months ending in December; excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.9 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The lower inflation readings over the second half of last year are welcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we will need to see continuing evidence to build confidence that inflation is moving down sustainably toward our goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Longer-term inflation expectations appear to remain well anchored, as reflected in a broad range of surveys of households, businesses, and forecasters, as well as measures from financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed’s monetary policy actions are guided by our mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I are acutely aware that high inflation imposes significant hardship, as it erodes purchasing power, especially for those least able to meet the higher costs of essentials like food, housing, and transportation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re highly attentive to the risks that high inflation poses to both sides of our mandate, and we’re strongly committed to returning inflation to our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Over the past two years, we have raised our policy rate by 5¼ percentage points, and we’ve decreased our securities holdings by more than $1.3 trillion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our restrictive stance of monetary policy is putting downward pressure on economic activity and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Committee decided at today’s meeting to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 5¼ to 5½ percent and to continue the process of significantly reducing our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We believe that our policy rate is likely at its peak for this tightening cycle and that, if the economy evolves broadly as expected, it will likely be appropriate to begin dialing back policy restraint at some point this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the economy has surprised forecasters in many ways since the pandemic, and ongoing progress toward our 2 percent inflation objective is not assured.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economic outlook is uncertain, and we remain highly attentive to inflation risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re prepared to maintain the current target range for the federal funds rate for longer if appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As labor market tightness has eased and progress on inflation has continued, the risks to achieving our employment and inflation goals are moving into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that reducing policy restraint too soon or too much could result in a reversal of the progress we’ve seen on inflation and ultimately require even tighter policy to get inflation back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, reducing policy restraint too late or too little could unduly weaken economic activity and employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In considering any adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will carefully assess the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Committee does not expect that it will be appropriate to reduce the target range until it has gained greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to make our decisions meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to bringing inflation back down to our 2 percent goal and to keeping longer-run—longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Restoring price stability is essential to set the stage for achieving maximum employment and stable prices over the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To conclude: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We at the Fed will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I look forward to our questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sorry—say that last part again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Okay.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Let me say that we have confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re—we’re looking for greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Implicitly, we do have confidence, and it has been increasing, but we want to get greater confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We want to see more good data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not that we’re looking for better data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—we’re looking at continuation of the good data that we’ve been seeing, and a good example is inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we have six months of good inflation data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s the question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the answer will come from some more data that’s also good data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It doesn’t—it’s not that the six-month data isn’t—isn’t low enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s really what we’re thinking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of, of growth, we’ve had strong growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, if you take a step back, we’ve had strong growth—very strong growth [in real GDP] last year—going right into the fourth quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And yet we’ve had a very strong labor market, and we’ve had inflation coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think—whereas a year ago, we, we were thinking that we needed to see some softening in economic activity—that hasn’t been the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think we, we look at—we look at stronger growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t look at it as a problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think, at this point, we want to see strong growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We want to see a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not looking for a weaker labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re looking for inflation to continue to come down, as it has been coming down for the last six months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No, I think it’s—I, I would say it, it seems—it seems to be the likely case that, that we will achieve that confidence, but we have to achieve it, and we haven’t yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so—I mean, it’s a good story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have six months of good inflation [readings].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But you can—and you know this—you can look behind those numbers, and you can see that a lot of it’s been coming from goods inflation, for example, and goods inflation running significantly negative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a reasonable assumption that, over time, goods inflation will flatten out—probably approximate zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That would mean the services sectors would have to contribute more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, in other words, what we care about is the aggregate number—not so much the composition.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we, we just need to see more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s where we are, as a Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We need to see more evidence that sort of confirms what we think we’re seeing and that tells us that we are on—gives us confidence that we’re on, on a path to—a sustainable path down to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, as you know, almost every participant on the Committee does believe that it will be appropriate to reduce rates and for, for—partly for the reasons that you say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we, we feel like inflation is coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Growth has been strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market is strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re—what we’re trying to do is identify a place where we’re really confident about inflation getting back down to 2 percent so that we can then begin the process of dialing back the restrictive level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, overall, I think—I think people do believe—and, as you know, the median participant wrote down three rate cuts this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I think to get to that place where we feel comfortable starting the process, we need some confirmation that inflation is, in fact, coming down sustainably to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, I—look, I think, as you know, we consult the range of Taylor rules and, and non-Taylor kind of rules.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We consult them regularly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re in our, our Tealbook, and, and they’re in all the materials that we look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, I don’t think we’ve ever been at a—at a place where we were—where we were setting policy by them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And there—depending on the rule, it will tell you different things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are many different formulations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Another way to think about it is, implicitly, is—so, in theory, of course, real rates go up if—holding all else equal—as inflation comes down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that doesn’t mean we can mechanically adjust policy as real rates—sorry—as inflation comes down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It doesn’t mean that at all, because, for one thing, we, we don’t know—we, we look at more than just the fed funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We look at—broadly—financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, in addition, we don’t know with great confidence where the neutral rate of interest is at any given time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that also doesn’t mean that we wait around for—to see, you know, the economy turn down, because that would be too late.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re really in a risk-management mode: of managing the risk—as I mentioned in my opening remarks—managing the risk that we move too soon and move too late.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think to move, which is—which is where almost everyone on the Committee is—is in favor of, of moving rates down this year—but the timing of that is going to be linked to our gaining confidence that inflation is on a sustainable path down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, I, I don’t know that we’ve worked out the particulars—statement language and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would just say, if you look at—you know, look at where, where 12-month inflation is, and it’s, you know, it’s still well above—core is 2.9 percent, for example—12-month—which is way down from where it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Very, very positive development—very fast decline—and, and, you know, the, the case is likely that it will continue to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, so that’s where—that’s where it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’re, you know, we’re wanting to see, you know, more data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So let me say that we’re not looking for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s not something we’re looking for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, yes, if you think about, you know—in, in the base case, the economy is performing well—the labor market remains strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we saw an unexpected weakening in, in—certainly in the labor market, that would certainly weigh on cutting sooner.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Absolutely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And if we saw inflation being stickier or higher or those sorts of things—would argue for moving later.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the base case, though, where, where the economy is healthy and we have, you know, we have ongoing growth—solid growth—we have a strong labor market—we have inflation coming down—that’s what people are writing their SEP [submissions] around.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And in that case, what we’re saying is, based on that, we think we can and should take advantage of that and, and be careful as we approach that question of when to begin to dial back restriction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re not—we’re not really at that stage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’re—we’re—there was no proposal to cut rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Some people did, you know, talk about their view of the rate path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would point you to the [December 2023] SEP as, as, you know, as good evidence of where people are, although it is—it is [now] one [FOMC meeting] cycle later.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we’re not—we’re not at a place of, of really working out those kinds of details, because we weren’t actively considering, you know, a—moving, moving the federal funds rate down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will say, there is a—there is a wide disparity—a healthy disparity—of views, and you see that in public, public statements, in the minutes, and the transcripts when they’re released every five years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we do have a healthy set of differences, and I think that’s actually essential for making good policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re also able to reach agreement, generally, because we listen to each other— we, we compromise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And even though not everybody loves what we do, they’re able to—for the most part—able to join in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To me, that’s a well-functioning public institution.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, so we’re not—you know, it’s not the pandemic, so we can actually rely on more, more traditional forms.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People are working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re getting wages, and, and the economy has largely reopened and is broadly normalizing, as you see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I wouldn’t say we’re looking at that, that sort of more innovative data as much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, you point to rents.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, of course, we follow the, the components of inflation very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Which would be: Goods inflation—I talked about that a little bit; you mentioned housing inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we think that’s coming, and we know it’s coming.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s just a question of when and, and how big it’ll be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—but that’s in, in everyone’s forecast, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that will—that will help.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But at the same time, we think goods inflation will probably—it’s been giving a lot of disinflation to the effort—and probably that declines over time, but it may well have some, some more time to run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, these—the supply chains are not perfectly back to where they were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, it takes time for the, the healing process to get into prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there may be still a tailwind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll find out with, with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we look at the things that relate to our mandate very carefully, and—as you would imagine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No, I wouldn’t—I wouldn’t say we’ve achieved that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I, I think we have—we have a ways to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation is still—you know, core inflation is still well above target on a 12-month basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Twelve months is our, our target, certainly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m encouraged, and we’re encouraged by the progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, we’re, we’re not—we’re not declaring victory at all at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think we have a ways to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s—I think you, you do see in the interest-sensitive parts of the economy—you do see, for example, housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You see the effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Your, your second question, though, really, I think, is important, and that is, a lot of this has come through—a lot of the disinflationary process has come through the healing of supply chains and also of the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’ve seen the—you know, that other set of factors is really different from other cycles and has brought that working with tighter, tighter policy, which has enabled the supply side to recover—I think is that, that mixture has been behind what has enabled this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, no—we really do think that we’re having an effect broadly across the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would point to the interest-sensitive parts of the economy as well as spending, generally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s a—it’s a joint story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s a complicated story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s—so I think it’s, it’s—of course, you know that it’s not something you can identify with any precision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But if you—a standard approach would be to take the nominal rate—5.3 percent, let’s say—and subtract sort of a, a forward measure of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If you do that—and there are many, many ways to calculate the neutral rate—but that’s one I like to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, you’re going to get to something that is materially above mainstream estimates of neutrality—of the neutral rate—you will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that, that won’t go on forever.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So a lot of the growth we’re seeing is not—is—it isn’t just a tug of war between, between interest rates and demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re getting, you know, more activity because of the—of labor market healing and supply chains healing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think the question is, when that peters out, I think the, the, you know, the, the restriction will show up probably more, more sharply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I think the labor market by many measures is at or nearing normal—but not totally back to normal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you pointed to one or more of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think, you know, job openings are not quite back to where they were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wages—wage increases, rather, are not quite back to where they—to where they would need to be in the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, I would look at it this way, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The, the economy is broadly normalizing, and so is the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that process will probably take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So wage setting is something that happens—it’s, it’s—you know, probably will take a couple of years to get all the way back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s okay.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s okay.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we do see—you saw today’s ECI reading—you know, the evidence is that, that wage increases are still at a healthy level—very healthy level—but they’re gradually moving back to levels that would be more associated—given, given assumptions about productivity, are more typically associated with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s, it’s an ongoing process—a healthy one—and, and, you know, I think we’re, we’re moving in the right direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think the, the labor market is—it—I don’t know if I’d—it’s rebalancing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Clearly, that the—there was a fairly severe imbalance between demand for workers and supply at the beginning of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we lost several million workers at the beginning of the pandemic from people dropping out of the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then when the economy reopened—you remember 2021—you had a severe labor shortage, and it was just—it was everywhere—panic on the part of businesses—couldn’t, couldn’t find people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, what’s happened is—we expected labor—the labor supply—labor market to come back quickly, and it didn’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And 2022 was a disappointing year, and, you know, we were kind of thinking, “Well, maybe we won’t get it back.” And then 2023, we did, as you know—so labor force participation came back strongly in ’23, and so did immigration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Immigration came to a halt during the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—and so those two forces have significantly lowered the temperature in the labor market to what is still a very strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s still a good labor market for wages and for finding a job, but it’s getting back into balance, and that’s what we want to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, one great way to look at that is what’s happening with, with wage increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you see it now across the, the major things that we—that we track.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It isn’t every quarter, but, overall, there’s a clear trend—still at high levels, but back down to where—what would be consistent with, with where we were before the pandemic and with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No, I think that that is a risk—the risk that inflation would, would reaccelerate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think the, the greater risk is that it would—that it would stabilize at a level meaningfully above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s, to me, more likely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, if—if inflation were to surprise by moving back up, that would—we would have to respond to that, and that would— that would be a surprise at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I have to tell you, that’s why we keep our options open here and why we’re not, you know, rushing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t think so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t—you know, that’s not what we think, but that’s the question we are asking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have to ask [that], and we want to get comfort on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll just have to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll—we look at those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Last year was a—was a, a surprise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I guess I would just say this—executive summary would be that growth is solid to strong over the course of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market—3.7 percent unemployment indicates that the labor market is strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve had just about two years now of, of unemployment under 4 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That hasn’t happened in 50 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s a good labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve seen inflation come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve talked about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’ve got six months of good inflation data and an expectation that there’s more to come.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this is a—this is a good situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Let’s be honest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is a—this is a good economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s looking in the rearview—the outlook—we do expect growth to moderate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, we have expected it for some time, and it hasn’t happened, but we do expect that it will moderate as supply chain and labor market normalization runs its course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market is rebalancing, as, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Job creation has slowed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The base of job growth has narrowed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, of course, 12-month inflation is, is above target and getting, you know, getting down closer to target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not guaranteed, but we do seem to be getting on track for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So those are the risks and, and questions we have to answer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, overall, this is a pretty good picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It, it is a good picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Your second question was—sorry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we—the thing is, we’re not looking for inflation to tap the 2 percent base once.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re looking for it to settle out over time at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the same thing is true if we have a month or two of lower—and we have that now—of, of inflation that’s annualized at a—at a lower level—that wouldn’t be good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not—you know, we’re not looking to have inflation anchor below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re looking to have it anchor at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if we do face those circumstances, then we’ll have to deal with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think—I think as of now, you know, the, the question, which—we want to take advantage of this situation and finish the job on inflation while keeping the labor market strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’ll point you to that language on your first question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we included that language in the statement to signal clearly that—with strong growth, strong labor market, inflation coming down—the Committee intends to move carefully as we consider when to begin to dial back the restrictive stance that we have in place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So if you take that to the current context—current context, we’re going to be data dependent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to be looking at this meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Based on the meeting today, I would tell you that I don’t think it’s likely that the Committee will reach a level of confidence by the time of the March meeting to identify March as the time to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s, that’s to be seen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I wouldn’t call—you know, when you say—when you ask me about “in the near term,” I’m hearing that as March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I would say I don’t think that’s—that’s, that’s probably not the most likely case or what we would call the base case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And your second question is— EDWARD LAWRENCE.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, that’s going to depend on the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The whole thing is, this is going to depend on the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to be looking at the economic data as it affects the outlook and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re going to make our decisions based on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it could wind up—you know, we’ll, we’ll have another SEP at the March meeting, and, and people will write down what they think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, in the end, it’s really going to depend on how the economy evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We talked about, there are risks that would cause us to go slower—for example, stronger inflation—more, more persistent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are risks that would cause us to—if they happen—that would cause us to go faster or—and sooner.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that would be a weakening in the labor market or, for that matter, very, very persuasive lower inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those are the kinds of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re just—we’re just going to be reacting to the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s the—that’s really the only way we can do this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So this is a really interesting question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think—my, my own view is—I think if you look, look back to the pandemic, you, you saw a spike in productivity as workers were laid off, and, and activity didn’t decline as fast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then you saw a deep trough of productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then, over the last—you saw high productivity last year, in ’23.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think we’re, we’re basically in the throes of getting through the pandemic economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the question will be, what, what is it that has changed the—you know, the productivity tends to be based on, you know, fundamental aspects of our economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It would take—you know, people talk about AI, but I would—my guess is that we may shake out and be back where we were, because I don’t—I’m not sure I see—work from home doesn’t seem like it’s a big productivity increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Or AI, artificial intelligence—generative it may be, but probably not in the short run—probably, maybe in the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I’m not—I’m not seeing why it would, but, you know, right—you know, right now I would say that productivity is kind of what falls out of the, the broader forces that are driving people in and out of the labor force and, and activity returning and supply chains getting fixed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s one way to look at it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So when we think about, you know—our, our statutory goals are maximum employment and price stability, and that’s what we’re targeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not targeting housing price inflation, the cost of housing, or any of those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those are very important things for people’s lives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But they’re not—you know, those are not the things we’re targeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re also well aware that when we cut rates at the beginning of the pandemic, for example, the housing, housing industry was helped more than any other industry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And when we raise rates, the housing industry can be hurt, because it’s a very interest-sensitive sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: On top of that, we have longer-run problems with the availability of housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we have a, a built-up set of cities, and, and, you know, people are moving further and further out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there’s—there hasn’t been enough housing built.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And these are not—these are not things that we have any tools to address.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, where it comes into play very specifically in our work is inflation, which is a combination.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s, it’s really rental inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re taking owners’ equivalent rent and then actual rent paid by tenants.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And you’re, you’re running that through the CPI calculation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Or the PCE [inflation] calculation—the one we look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And what that’s telling you is that market rents are increasing at a much lower rate or even being flat and that that will show up in inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It has to as long as that remains the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My response is what I started with, which is that our, our job—the job Congress has given us is price stability and maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Price stability is absolutely essential for people’s lives, most importantly for—well, not most importantly—most, mostly for people at the lower end of the income spectrum who are living at the edges—at the margins.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so someone—for someone like that, high inflation in the—in the necessities of life—right away, you’re in trouble, whereas even middle-class people have some, you know, some scope to absorb higher costs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we have to get—it’s our job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s what society has asked us to do, is to get inflation down, and the tools that we use to do it are interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s how we think about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I would start by saying that balance sheet runoff so far has gone very well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And as the process has continued, you know, we’re getting to that time where questions are beginning to come into greater focus about the pace of runoff and all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So at this meeting, we did have some discussion of the balance sheet, and we’re planning to begin in-depth discussions of balance sheet issues at our next meeting in March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So those, those questions are all coming into scope now, and we’re focusing on them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’re, we’re at the beginning of that process, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yes, we do—we see those as independent tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so they don’t—for example, if you’re—if you’re normalizing policy, you might be reducing rates but continuing to run off the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In both cases, that’s normalization, but from a strict monetary policy standpoint, you could say we’re loosening along with tightening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that, that could happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not something we’re planning or thinking about, but right now, we’re thinking about getting to a place where—we’re going to see the balance sheet runoff to continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re watching it carefully, and, as I said, we’ll—we’ll be looking into that as a Committee starting in March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m, I’m not in a position to put a number on it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m just going to say—and it’s not that we don’t have any confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, we have growing confidence, but not to the point where we—where we feel like—it’s a highly consequential decision to start the process of, of dialing back on restriction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we want to get that right, and we feel like the strong economy, strong labor market, inflation coming down—it gives us the ability to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We think that’s the best way we can serve the public, because, ultimately, we, we’ve made a lot of progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We just want to make sure that we do get the job done in a sustainable way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s how we’re thinking about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of when that’ll be, you know, that, that’ll all come out of our communications, and, you know, we won’t—we won’t keep that a secret.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Not a decision that we’ve made, but I, I wouldn’t think we’d, we’d be—we wouldn’t be taking a position that it’s got to go to zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, if it—if it were to stabilize at a different level—but that’s, that’s not a decision that we’ve made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s what we’ll be talking about at the March meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: A whole range of issues will be briefed up, and the Committee will get into—get into all of the issues that will be arising over the course of the next, let’s say, year or so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t have a stance on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s not something I’m focused on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: [We’re] focused on doing our jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have—this year is going to be a highly consequential year for, for the Fed and for monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re, all of us, very buckled down, focused on doing our jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I—you know, we’re going to do—we’ll update our, our inflation forecasts at the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You referred to the December meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s, you know, three months old [by March], so it might be lower now, given the data we’ve gotten.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, look, as I mentioned, we’re going to be reacting to the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If, if we get—if we get very strong inflation data and it, it kicks back up, then it’ll—then we’ll go slower or later or both.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If we got really good inflation data soon, that would matter for both the—that, that would tell us that, that we could go sooner and perhaps go faster.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re just going to be—but, of course, we’ll weigh that with all the other factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re setting policy based on the totality of, of the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, I think if we—if we came to the view that, that inflation were—that the six-month inflation numbers, which are very close to 2 [percent], were, in “PCE world”—if we came to—if that’s—if we thought that is really where we’re going to be, then, yes, our policy would be in a different place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It would.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, that’s the whole point is, we’re trying to get comfortable and gain confidence that that is where—that inflation is on a sustainable path down to 2 percent or toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah, so it’s been—it’s been interesting that confidence surveys have been weak, at a time when unemployment has been low—very low, historically low—for a couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And—but, nonetheless, that’s been the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’ve asked ourselves why that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, you know, one obvious answer—we don’t pretend to have perfect wisdom on this—is—but one obvious answer is that the price level is high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So prices went up much more than 2 percent for year—per year for a couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And people are going to the store, and they’re paying much more for the basics of life than they were two years ago—three years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And they’re not happy about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s fine that inflation is coming down, but the price—the prices they’re paying are still high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that, that is what—that, that has to be some part of why people are unhappy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And they’re, they’re right to be unhappy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, this is why we need to keep price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s why we need to do our jobs—so that people don’t have to deal with things like this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of [surveys]—you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In, in recent, recent surveys, a couple of—you’ve seen a couple of significant increases in, in consumer confidence or, or happiness with the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I guess that’s a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That can—that can support spending—can support economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s some evidence of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it is—it is a fact that we have seen, you know, a meaningful increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think levels of confidence are still maybe not as high as they’ve been at various times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But it’s—they certainly have come up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, yes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m, I’m a big believer that—yes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we, we do meet with outside groups who come from all different parts of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I always feel like you—I mean, I spent most of my life in the private sector looking at companies—individual companies—individual management teams—and then building out from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so, starting with GDP data is—and working into what’s actually affecting people’s lives is—is challenging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s very hard.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I really like anecdotal data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In addition, as you know, the 12 Reserve Banks have really the best network of anyone.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In all their Districts, they’re talking to, you know, not just the business community, but the educational, medical, all, all—you know, nonprofit community.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They have arms into all of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so when they come back—that’s what goes into the Beige Book.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But they come back, and what each Reserve Bank president does is, during the outlook go-around, they’ll say, “In my District . . .” And they’ll talk about 100 conversations they—not—they won’t talk—they, they will give you input, based on 100 conversations that they’ve had with people of all different walks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it’s—I personally find it very helpful in understanding what’s going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And also, I think you hear things before they show up in the data sometimes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, if you—if you look back at the last—not this Beige Book, but the one before, it was more—there was a lot of “slower activity.” I think that, that what you’re hearing now is, is, things are picking up a bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re hearing—not, not in every District and not every, every person that we talk to, but you’re—overall, it feels like you’re hearing things picking up at the margin.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what comes through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I’m not so worried about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, it’s—again, we’ve had inflation come down without a slow economy and without, you know, important increases in, in unemployment, and there’s no reason why we should want to get in the way of that process, if it’s going to continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I, I am—you know, I think—I think declining inflation—continued declines in inflation are, are really the main thing we’re looking at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, we want the labor market to remain strong, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t have a growth mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve got a, a maximum-employment mandate and a, a price-stability mandate, and those are the two things we look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Growth only matters to the extent it influences our achievement of those two—of those two mandates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you very much.
